questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Meaning of Rights' refers to.
questions.a: Rights are reasonable claims of persons recognised by society and sanctioned by law, which enable individuals to develop their personality and live with dignity, backed by the authority of the state.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Meaning of Rights'.
questions.a: Rights are claims that are recognised by society and enforced by the state; they are essential for the full development of individuals and the protection of their dignity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Meaning of Rights' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Meaning of Rights

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Fundamental Rights: An Overview' refers to.
questions.a: Fundamental Rights are the basic rights guaranteed by Part III (Articles 12 to 35) of the Indian Constitution to all citizens, which are enforceable by courts and are essential for the development of individuals and the democratic functioning of the country.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Fundamental Rights: An Overview'.
questions.a: The Indian Constitution guarantees six categories of Fundamental Rights that are enforceable by courts and cannot be violated by the state, forming the cornerstone of Indian democracy.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Fundamental Rights: An Overview' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Fundamental Rights

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Right to Equality' refers to.
questions.a: The Right to Equality, guaranteed by Articles 14 to 18, establishes equality before law and equal protection of laws, prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, or place of birth, and abolishes untouchability and titles.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Right to Equality'.
questions.a: The Right to Equality ensures that all citizens are treated equally by the law, prohibits discrimination, and abolishes social evils like untouchability and the conferment of titles.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Right to Equality' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Right to Equality (Articles 14-18)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Right to Freedom' refers to.
questions.a: The Right to Freedom, guaranteed by Articles 19 to 22, provides for six freedoms of citizens (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession), protection against arbitrary arrest and detention, and safeguards in cases of preventive detention.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Right to Freedom'.
questions.a: The Right to Freedom guarantees essential personal and political freedoms to citizens, while allowing reasonable restrictions in the interest of public order, security, and morality.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Right to Freedom' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Right against Exploitation' refers to.
questions.a: The Right against Exploitation, guaranteed by Articles 23 and 24, prohibits traffic in human beings and forced labour (begar), and bans the employment of children below the age of fourteen years in factories, mines, or hazardous occupations.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Right against Exploitation'.
questions.a: The Right against Exploitation protects vulnerable sections of society by prohibiting human trafficking, forced labour, and child labour in hazardous occupations.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Right against Exploitation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Right to Freedom of Religion' refers to.
questions.a: The Right to Freedom of Religion, guaranteed by Articles 25 to 28, provides freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise, and propagate religion, while allowing the state to regulate secular activities and ensure public order, morality, and health.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Right to Freedom of Religion'.
questions.a: India is a secular state where all religions are treated equally; citizens have the freedom to profess, practise, and propagate any religion, subject to public order, morality, and health.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Right to Freedom of Religion' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Cultural and Educational Rights' refers to.
questions.a: Cultural and Educational Rights, guaranteed by Articles 29 and 30, protect the interests of minorities by allowing them to conserve their culture, language, and script, and by giving them the right to establish and administer educational institutions.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Cultural and Educational Rights'.
questions.a: The Constitution protects the cultural and educational interests of minorities, both religious and linguistic, ensuring that they can preserve their identity and establish educational institutions of their choice.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Cultural and Educational Rights' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Right to Constitutional Remedies' refers to.
questions.a: The Right to Constitutional Remedies, guaranteed by Article 32, allows a citizen to approach the Supreme Court directly for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights through writs such as habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari, and quo warranto.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Right to Constitutional Remedies'.
questions.a: Article 32 makes Fundamental Rights enforceable by empowering citizens to approach the Supreme Court directly, which is why Dr. Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Right to Constitutional Remedies' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32)

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Directive Principles of State Policy' refers to.
questions.a: Directive Principles of State Policy, contained in Part IV (Articles 36 to 51), are guidelines for the state in making laws and policies, aimed at establishing social and economic justice, and are not enforceable by courts but are fundamental to governance.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Directive Principles of State Policy'.
questions.a: Directive Principles are non-justiciable directions to the state to promote social and economic welfare, inspired by the Irish Constitution, and are fundamental in the governance of the country.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Directive Principles of State Policy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36-51)

concepts.title: Relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles' refers to.
questions.a: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are complementary to each other; Fundamental Rights are justiciable rights that protect individual liberty, while Directive Principles are non-justiciable goals that guide the state towards social and economic justice, and together they form the conscience of the Constitution.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles'.
questions.a: Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are not contradictory but complementary, aiming together to establish a just and welfare society, with courts harmoniously interpreting them.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Relationship between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles
